stories.summary: Around 2007-08, before dating apps, gay men in Bombay found partners through classified websites. Vikram Doctor told Amit about a scheme the police were running. A cop would pose as someone looking for love and suggest meeting at Matunga station for coffee. When the man arrived, the cops grabbed him and extorted money by threatening to tell his parents or wife. Sometimes they took him into an ATM and emptied his account. Amit wrote about it in a Mint column.
stories.insight: Outlawing a victimless act gives the state a ready-made lever of shame, and someone will use it to make money. Amit's point is that this is not a few bad cops but incentives at work. Once the law went, the racket became impossible.
stories.quote: To me this is not a bunch of bad cops. To me this is the incentives, this is the nature of the state.

stories.summary: In 2003 Amit read about Armin Meiwes, a 42-year-old man in Rotenburg, Germany. His neighbours called him normal, but he had fantasised about eating a human being since he was eight. He advertised for a well-built young man who wanted to be eaten. Bernd Brandes answered, saying he had always fantasised about being eaten. Brandes consented at every stage, mostly on camera. He took twenty sleeping pills and some schnapps, and his penis was cut off and cooked. Meiwes read a Star Trek novel while Brandes bathed. Meiwes then killed him with a cleaver, froze the body and ate it over many days with olive oil and garlic. Cannibalism is not a crime in Germany; murder is.
stories.insight: With documented consent on both sides, the case breaks a simple 'were rights infringed?' test. It raises hard questions: does consenting to be killed and eaten prove mental illness, and if so, is the killer insane too? Sanity is a continuum, so who gets to draw the line?
stories.quote: And this is almost a clear cut case where it seems that both these people must be insane by some kind of legal definition. But there are many cases where it is not so clear cut and there is a continuum between sanity and insanity.

stories.topic: How the Sugar Lobby Rewrote America's Diet
stories.summary: Retelling the history from the show's diabetes episode, Amit says the sugar lobby spent heavily on researchers from Harvard and elsewhere. Their influential studies used bad methodology, mistook correlation for causation, blamed fat and cleared sugar. In 1977 the top US dietary body issued guidelines saying sugar was fine and fat was evil. Charts of the obesity epidemic show it exploding from then, as people followed the guidelines into processed-sugar junk food.
stories.insight: State guidance can be captured by lobbies and built on bad science, and because everyone follows it, the damage scales. Amit does not conclude that sugar should be banned. He concludes the state should stay out, since its knowledge is never good enough.
stories.quote: But its knowledge was not good enough. And the matter should just have been left to individuals to decide.

stories.summary: Amit has had alcohol in Gujarat, which has prohibition. He has also had it in Lahore while visiting Pakistan, which has prohibition too, and found a flourishing black market for alcohol and drugs there.
stories.insight: Two prohibition regimes, and the same outcome as everywhere else: demand doesn't disappear, it goes underground.
stories.quote: Because it should never have been banned in the first place. I might not partake of them, but other people have agency, and if they wish to do so, that's the way it is.

stories.topic: Five Years at the Poker Table
stories.summary: Amit played poker professionally for five years and spent a lot of time in casinos. In all that time he never once played against the house; he has never put a single rupee on a roulette table, because it is a losing proposition. He also watched gambling addiction destroy lives. When people close to him got hooked, he tried to intervene and failed.
stories.insight: If even loved ones can't talk someone out of an addiction, a blunt state ban won't do better; social problems have to be solved by society. His refusal to bet against the house also shows his wider point that gambling is just weighing probabilities.
stories.quote: In the case of people close to me, I have tried to make interventions and I have failed because addiction is addiction.

stories.topic: Telling an MP Why Hate-Speech Laws Backfire
stories.summary: At a recent literary festival, Amit shared a stage with an MP who had brought a bill against hate speech on platforms. He told the MP the intent was beautiful. But after twenty-five years of writing about free speech, he warned that such laws always end up being used to attack dissenters.
stories.insight: Intent doesn't decide how a law is used; whoever holds power does. Vague laws like 295A and 153A mean anyone can be locked up depending on how they are interpreted.
stories.quote: I get the intent. It's very beautiful. But I've been writing about free speech for twenty five years and let me tell you something. Laws against hate speech will always be used against free speech.

recommendations.context: Ajay's closing recommendation: 'a person and a story.' Turing helped crack the German Enigma machines, which was vital to the Allied victory in World War II, and imagined computers before they existed. His life was destroyed by old British laws against homosexuality.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says studying Turing's life 'will reshape your moral calculus' by showing what state coercion over private matters actually costs. Amit adds that Turing's story stands for that of homosexuals through most of human history.

recommendations.item: Bootleggers and Baptists—The Education of a Regulatory Economist
recommendations.creator: Bruce Yandle
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'a great essay by the regulatory economist' in the chapter on alcohol prohibition.
recommendations.reason: It explains why prohibition persists. The moral crusader (the Baptist) and the black-market supplier (the bootlegger) both want the ban, so they work towards the same end even without openly colluding.

recommendations.item: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's review of the film Raees, mentioned while discussing Bootleggers and Baptists.
recommendations.reason: The film shows Shah Rukh Khan's bootlegger fighting a goody-goody anti-alcohol politician. Amit argues this makes no sense, because their incentives are aligned.

recommendations.item: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit cites the liver doctor's point from this episode at the start of the alcohol chapter.
recommendations.reason: Abby Philips argues that even an occasional glass of alcohol is bad for you: whatever a glass of wine does for the heart, the liver damage outweighs it.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit tells listeners to 'check that out' while discussing sugar.
recommendations.reason: It lays out how the sugar lobby funded flawed research and how the 1977 US dietary guidelines fed the obesity epidemic.

recommendations.item: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped (2008)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit opens by noting he has written many pieces arguing the state should not punish victimless crimes; this one is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It is the written version of the episode's core argument.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as background to the episode.
recommendations.reason: One of Amit's earlier pieces listed alongside the episode's themes, for readers who want more of his writing on them.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes; Amit makes the same argument in the gambling chapter.
recommendations.reason: It argues that every life choice, from marriage to jobs to stocks, is a bet weighed on probabilities, so singling out gambling for stigma makes little sense.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: One of the columns Amit says he wrote on gambling and promised to link while recalling his poker years.
recommendations.reason: Amit has seen gambling addiction destroy lives up close; his columns deal with that dark side honestly, without asking for bans.

recommendations.creator: Aella
recommendations.context: Amit calls it one of his favourite Twitter accounts, in the prostitution chapter.
recommendations.reason: Aella is an openly happy sex worker who is also 'incredible at data' and runs large-scale surveys. She is a living counter to the assumption that sex work is always coerced.

recommendations.creator: Aella
recommendations.context: Aella's Substack, mentioned alongside her Twitter account.
recommendations.reason: One of the few newsletters Amit has paid $100 a year for, because it is 'so packed with insight' about gender relations.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Mint column on Bombay police extorting gay men, based on a tip from Vikram Doctor.
recommendations.reason: A concrete case of a victimless 'crime' becoming a tool for police extortion.

recommendations.item: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
recommendations.context: Amit brings it up after Ajay's point about no-fault divorce.
recommendations.reason: Three scholars propose innovative, intuitive metrics for women's empowerment. Amit's own opening metric was rising divorce rates.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates (2008)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes; Amit argues the same point in the episode.
recommendations.reason: Rising divorce rates mean more women can walk out of bad marriages, which is something to celebrate rather than lament.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay points listeners to it after arguing that 8% GDP growth is the greatest instrument for women's emancipation.
recommendations.reason: Anyone who cares about women in India should sign on to the economic growth project instead of 'bleeding heart things' that achieve nothing.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended together with Why Freedom Matters.
recommendations.reason: It explains how economic development actually happens, which Ajay sees as the real path to empowering the disempowered.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay draws on 'Kelkar and Shah' for the idea of state capability as a finite budget.
recommendations.reason: It gives the framework for why India, with little state capability, should focus on a few core functions and not waste capacity on policing private choices.

core_ideas.explanation: Being illegal is not the same as being wrong. For Amit, a crime is infringing someone's rights, such as murdering them or stealing their property. The state's job is to stop such infringements, not to engineer society to its liking. So-called 'victimless crimes' are not crimes at all, just acts the state has chosen to outlaw.
core_ideas.quote: If there is a crime, there must be a victim.

core_ideas.concept: Three objections to banning victimless crimes
core_ideas.explanation: 1. Moral: consenting adults should be free to deal with each other however they like, in the bedroom, the marketplace or the public square. 2. Practical: a ban doesn't end demand, it brings in an underworld with coercion and fraud, and still fails to deliver the intended outcome. 3. Power: the state's monopoly on coercion should be limited, because whoever holds it will remake society according to their own values.
core_ideas.quote: But the point is the person you hate most in the world could be in power tomorrow, and they'll pass laws according to their values.

core_ideas.explanation: Bruce Yandle's idea: every prohibition has a moraliser (the Baptist) demanding the ban on ethical grounds, and a bootlegger who profits by selling lower-quality, unregulated supply on the black market. Hooch tragedies follow. The two look like enemies but want the same thing.
core_ideas.quote: The Baptist wants alcohol banned, so he can do his virtue signaling, and the bootlegger wants alcohol banned so he can make money on the black market.

core_ideas.explanation: Economists judge how well a ban is enforced by the black-market price premium. But a high premium also signals huge profits to criminals and draws them in. So winning in the short run builds a bigger, better-organised underworld in the long run.
core_ideas.quote: the measure of successful enforcement is that The price of the forbidden substances should be high. But that very fact, high prices of illegal alcohol or illegal drugs kicks off greater energy by private people to engage in entry strategies.

core_ideas.explanation: A lone criminal can only do so much. Prohibitions give crime the scale to build firms with large teams and complex operations. India's import barriers created smuggling, smuggling became a giant business, and Haji Mastan's gangs grew out of it. Amit adds that import duties are themselves a victimless crime. Where the state bans things, its low-paid police also collect hafta from the underworld and from ordinary offenders.
core_ideas.quote: It is better for us to have lone rangers and solo creators in the world of crime.

core_ideas.explanation: Legal activity is visible, so it can be regulated. Amit argues match-fixing happens because betting is illegal: the underworld runs it, its money flows go unwatched, and corruption follows. Imagine instead betting through a bank account at HDFC or IDFC, the way you hold a demat account for shares, with only light-touch regulation against fraud. The same logic applies to brothels, worker rights and health care in sex work.

Every decision is a bet based on an intuitive sense of probabilities: talking to someone in a bar, marrying, picking a job, buying a house, investing in stocks. If gambling means weighing probabilities and betting on your best judgment, then everything is gambling, and singling out some forms for stigma is incoherent.
core_ideas.quote: Everything we do is gambling and we should not necessarily stigmatise certain forms of gambling.

core_ideas.concept: Drugs as a public-health issue, not a crime
core_ideas.explanation: Marijuana is less harmful than alcohol or cigarettes and far less harmful than sugar. Yet America's war on drugs soaked up police resources, built a vast underworld, hit African Americans hardest and did not stop drug use. Parts of Europe that allow drugs have seen no ill effects. Ajay says the conversation belongs between parents and children, or in public health, with the state staying out.
core_ideas.quote: this should be the conversations between moms and their kids, or it should be a public health issue.

core_ideas.concept: Sex work is a choice of the best available option
core_ideas.explanation: A sex worker sells her services just as writers, economists, carpenters and plumbers sell theirs. If someone chose it, it was the best option they had. Amit says India's Immoral Traffic Prevention Act defines prostitution as 'sexual exploitation or abuse,' which leaves consent out and confuses prostitution with trafficking. Coercion must be outlawed, but the way to prevent it is to keep the trade above ground.
core_ideas.quote: if someone has chosen to be a prostitute, they have done so because it is the best option open to them and now it is up to you to contemplate how bad the other options must be.

core_ideas.concept: Self-ownership and the right to end one's life
core_ideas.explanation: For Locke, the core right is self-ownership, and all other rights flow from it. If I own myself, I also have the right to end my life. Suicide is a serious social problem, and friends should help someone out of that dark place, but the state shouldn't criminalise it. Euthanasia raises a separate caution: where state capacity is low, as in India, people could misuse it to kill elders for their property.
core_ideas.quote: If your friend wants to off themselves, it is your duty as a friend, if you want to call yourself a friend, to help them out of that dark place. Right? At the same time, it is my right to off myself if I want to.

core_ideas.concept: Free speech has only one limit: direct incitement
core_ideas.explanation: Speech becomes criminal only when it directly incites harm. Saying 'Jaake Amit ko maaro' is wrong because the beating itself is a crime. Otherwise even hate speech should stay legal. Laws like 295A and 153A sound well-meant, but they can be interpreted to lock up anyone.
core_ideas.quote: Always and everywhere the state will use anti free speech laws to attack dissenters.

core_ideas.concept: Icky problems: moral instinct versus reason
core_ideas.explanation: Two thought experiments. Someone has sex with a chicken they bought and are about to kill and eat. Two adult siblings have sex and won't have children. Instinct says both are wrong, but reason finds no victim and no answer to 'why?'. Our moral instincts come from prehistoric programming we don't understand. So when the powerful want to outlaw something because it 'feels wrong,' that is a reason for more suspicion, not less.
core_ideas.quote: Because rationally it is not wrong, but our moral instincts take us in an another direction.

core_ideas.concept: Even the best states execute innocent people
core_ideas.explanation: Roughly 5% of people executed in advanced economies are later believed to have been innocent, despite the highest standards of evidence and the strongest state capability anywhere. India's failure rate must be far worse, so convictions deserve scepticism. Using such a flawed tool against people's private choices invites disaster.
core_ideas.quote: And there, one in twenty is actually innocent, and the state went and caught the wrong guy or did some horrible things.

core_ideas.concept: State capability is a finite budget
core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Kelkar and Shah: India has very little state capability, and it grows slowly. Rich countries like Sweden or the UK can afford to spend it widely; India must focus on a few basics such as defence, monetary policy, criminal justice, financial regulation and tax. Ajay estimates that is 50 to 100 years of work. Amit adds that victimless crimes shouldn't be on the list anyway, and the state should first make the rule of law real.
core_ideas.quote: when you have very little capability, the wise thing to do is to focus that capability on a few primordial and important problems

core_ideas.concept: Means and ends: give people the power to walk away
core_ideas.explanation: If you care about wives beaten by drunk husbands, banning alcohol won't help. What helps is no-fault divorce: easy, frictionless, codified, with jointly created wealth split equally. That gives the abused spouse the power to leave and changes the husband's incentives. For the same reason Amit treats rising divorce rates as a sign of women's empowerment, and notes that America's no-fault divorce, which he credits to Reagan, was very good for women.
core_ideas.quote: So just an emotional outrage is the surest way of getting to a wrong answer.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that the biggest driver of women's status in India is 8% GDP growth, so anyone who cares about women should back the growth project. Amit extends this to every marginalised group. Financial ability is what lets people walk away from bad situations.
core_ideas.quote: the greatest instrument for the emancipation and the status of women is eight percent GDP growth.

core_ideas.concept: Blow oxygen on the spark of doubt
core_ideas.explanation: Decriminalising homosexuality and allowing no-fault divorce show mainstream thinking was once completely wrong, and that removing the state worked well. Once you accept that, you should question other accepted uses of state power, such as drug laws.
core_ideas.quote: then I think we owe it to ourselves to blow oxygen on the spark of doubt in our hearts about the other things that we accept as conventional wisdom.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on India's old law against suicide: 'It was the one crime for which you got punished if you failed to commit it.'

Amit's only time smoking up, circa 1995, in the back seat of a car with a friend and 'a great world famous guitarist I won't name because it'll seem like too much of a humble brag.' The punchline: 'I felt nothing.'

Amit explains 'we are all gamblers' using Pi, who had just been on Ajay's lap. Putting him there was a bet: the chance he disrupts the shoot weighed against the joy and 'the oxytocin flooding through you.'
After Amit says he 'entirely supports' the black market for alcohol and drugs in Lahore, teetotaller Ajay replies: 'I will defend unto death your right to say certain things and do certain things.'
Amit on import duties: 'I buy something in America, I bring it here, and I sell it to a friend. And immediately it is a crime because I haven't paid the hafta to the state.'
Telling the cannibal story, Amit notes the body was eaten with olive oil and garlic: 'I don't know why there was no salt, perhaps a human flesh has natural salt like bacon does.'
Arguing for legal, regulated brothels run by proper organisations, Amit adds: 'I don't think HDFC or IDFC will do it, but you get what I'm saying.'
Amit on 'whore' as an insult: 'Like which of us is not a whore in some way or the other if you use the term in that manner.'
Amit read a Twitter rant listing five things Ronald Reagan got wrong, 'and as I was reading through them I realized that he got all of them right.' One of them was no-fault divorce.
Ajay's description of India's state capability: 'we have a teensy-weensy amount of state capability.'
John Locke's idea of self-ownership: Amit calls it the root right from which life, free speech and property flow, and uses it to argue for a right to end one's life.
Thoreau's 'lives of quiet desperation,' used for people who had to hide their sexuality while it was criminalised.
Bruce Yandle's 'Bootleggers and Baptists,' and how the Shah Rukh Khan film Raees got it backwards by making the bootlegger and the anti-alcohol politician enemies.
Haji Mastan's gangs, cited by Ajay as products of the smuggling economy that India's import barriers created.
Sections 295A and 153A, India's laws against spreading religious discord, which Amit says can be interpreted to lock up anyone.

Definitions compared: the Oxford dictionary calls prostitution 'engaging in sexual activity with someone for payment,' while India's Immoral Traffic Prevention Act calls it 'the sexual exploitation or abuse of persons for commercial purposes.'
Alzheimer's being called 'type three diabetes' by some, mentioned by Amit to show how many harms are traced back to sugar.
